.title: Liquidity *explained*
.yt_title: Liquidity Explained – Stop Hunts, Equal Highs/Lows & Sweep vs. Real Breakout on Gold
.chapters[0].title: Liquidity explained
.chapters[0].segs[0].say: Sound familiar? You put your stop just below a low, price spikes right into it – and then turns in your direction. That's not bad luck. That's liquidity.
.chapters[0].segs[1].say: In this video we'll look at where liquidity sits on the chart, how a stop hunt plays out, why equal highs and equal lows matter so much – and how to tell a sweep from a real breakout.
.chapters[0].segs[2].say: Important up front: this is educational content, not investment advice. Trading involves risk of loss. Practise new strategies on a demo account first.
.chapters[1].title: What is *liquidity*?
.chapters[1].hook: This is where most traders' stops sit
.chapters[1].segs[0].say: Liquidity sounds complicated, but it's simple: it's the places on the chart where a lot of orders are waiting. And most of them are stop-loss orders.
.chapters[1].segs[1].say: The market rises and forms a clear high. Everyone sees it, everyone draws it.
.chapters[1].segs[2].say: Then comes a pullback, and a clear low forms.
.chapters[1].segs[3].say: Above the high, the sellers' stops pile up – plus the buy orders of traders waiting for a breakout.
.chapters[1].segs[4].say: Below the low sit the buyers' stops. Exactly where most textbooks tell you to put your stop.
.chapters[1].segs[5].say: Why does that matter? Big market players need someone on the other side of their positions. Triggered stops provide exactly those orders. That's why these areas often act like a magnet for price.
.chapters[2].title: The *stop hunt*
.chapters[2].hook: How a stop hunt plays out on gold
.chapters[2].segs[0].say: Now let's look at what happens when price goes and takes that liquidity. This is called a stop hunt or liquidity sweep.
.chapters[2].segs[1].say: The market drops and forms a low.
.chapters[2].segs[2].say: Price comes back to roughly the same level once more. Now there are a lot of stops sitting below these lows.
.chapters[2].segs[3].say: Then a candle spikes below with a long wick. The stops get triggered – that's the sweep.
.chapters[2].segs[4].say: What matters is what happens next: price immediately returns above the old low. The sellers who got stopped out or went short there are now on the wrong side.
.chapters[2].segs[5].say: Often a strong impulse follows in the other direction. But careful: a sweep alone is not a trade idea yet. It's only the first clue.
.chapters[3].title: Equal *highs*
.chapters[3].segs[0].say: A particularly strong magnet is equal highs and equal lows. Many traders see them as safe resistance. In reality it's often the opposite.
.chapters[3].segs[1].say: Here gold rises and forms a high.
.chapters[3].segs[2].say: After a pullback, price runs right back up to the same level – and turns away again. A textbook double top.
.chapters[3].segs[3].say: Now there are twice as many stops and breakout orders above this line. The cleaner the highs, the more liquidity builds up there.
.chapters[3].segs[4].say: And then it happens: a wick shoots above the highs, takes the stops – but the candle closes back below. The breakout buyers are trapped.
.chapters[3].segs[5].say: Shortly after, price breaks below the last low. A break of structure to the downside confirms that the sellers have taken over.
.chapters[3].segs[6].say: The sell-off often keeps going until it reaches the next liquidity below. With equal lows, it works exactly the other way round.
.chapters[4].title: Sweep or *breakout*?
.chapters[4].hook: Sweep or real breakout? How to tell
.chapters[4].segs[0].say: Of course, not every break above a high is a sweep. Sometimes the breakout is real. So the key question is: how do you tell the difference?
.chapters[4].segs[1].say: Again we see several highs at the same level. Here too, liquidity sits above the line.
.chapters[4].segs[2].say: This time a candle with a big body closes clearly above the highs. No long wick, no quick drop back.
.chapters[4].segs[3].say: Price comes back to the old line but stays above it. The former resistance now holds as support. That's called a retest.
.chapters[4].segs[4].say: After that, the move continues. That's the difference: with a sweep, price returns quickly. With a real breakout, it closes above and holds the level.
.chapters[4].segs[5].say: If you're unsure, wait. One or two candles of patience cost you little – an entry in the wrong direction costs more.
.chapters[5].title: *Remember*
.chapters[5].segs[1].say: With a sweep, only the wick spikes beyond the level, and price comes back quickly.
.chapters[5].segs[2].say: With a breakout, the candle closes beyond it, and the level holds.
.chapters[6].title: Liquidity in the *setup*
.chapters[6].hook: From sweep to trade idea in 4 steps
.chapters[6].segs[0].say: Finally, let's put it all together. This is how a sweep can become the starting point for a well-thought-out trade idea.
.chapters[6].segs[1].say: The five-minute chart is correcting lower, while the higher-timeframe trend points up.
.chapters[6].segs[2].say: The stops sit below the last low. A wick takes them out – the sweep.
.chapters[6].segs[3].say: Then a candle closes above the last lower high. The change of character shows that the buyers are back.
.chapters[6].segs[4].say: The impulse leaves a fair value gap in the discount area. That's where you wait for the pullback.
.chapters[6].segs[5].say: The entry comes in the gap, and the stop goes below the sweep low. The market has already taken the liquidity there.
.chapters[6].segs[6].say: If the plan works, the next target is often the liquidity above the highs. But this setup can fail too – the stop always belongs in the plan.
.chapters[7].title: The *summary*
.chapters[7].segs[1].say: Liquidity sits where lots of stops sit: above highs and below lows.
.chapters[7].segs[2].say: Equal highs and equal lows aren't safe resistance – they're a magnet for price.
.chapters[7].segs[3].say: A sweep is a wick beyond the level with a fast return. A real breakout closes beyond it and holds on the retest.
.chapters[7].segs[4].say: A sweep alone isn't enough. Wait for a change of character as confirmation.
.chapters[7].segs[5].say: And don't put your stop where everyone else puts theirs. Risk only one to two percent of your account per trade.
.chapters[8].segs[0].say: If you want to see liquidity live on the gold chart every day: join our free gold group on Telegram. You'll find the link in the description. Our bootcamp with fifty-five lessons and daily trade ideas are waiting for you there too. See you in the next video!
